studies.headline: Trouble Reading Small Print May Quietly Undermine Heart Patients' Recovery
studies.the_study: Researchers followed 351 older adults hospitalized with cardiovascular disease across multiple Japanese hospitals who were taking part in cardiac rehabilitation. Nearly a third (31.9%) reported difficulty reading small print, and those patients were far less likely to advance through the stages of behavior change during their hospital stay (odds ratio 0.31). Patients who did make that behavioral progress had a markedly lower risk of being rehospitalized for a major cardiac or stroke event within a year (hazard ratio 0.37).
studies.why_it_matters: Much of what patients learn about managing heart disease after discharge comes in printed form — medication lists, diet sheets, exercise plans — and an unaddressed vision problem may silently block the self-care that prevents a return trip to the hospital.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you struggle to read medication labels or handouts, say so out loud during a hospital stay — ask for large-print materials, verbal teaching, or a teach-back session, and get your vision checked. Difficulty with small print isn't a minor inconvenience; it may affect how well you can act on your discharge instructions.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For discharge planners, cardiac rehab staff, and family caregivers: a one-question screen about reading small print may identify patients who need their education delivered differently. Consider reviewing written instructions aloud with the patient and confirming understanding before discharge rather than assuming the paperwork was read.
studies.caveats: Observational cohort — cannot prove that fixing vision problems improves outcomes; vision difficulty was self-reported rather than measured; conducted in Japanese hospitals among cardiac rehabilitation patients, so findings may not generalize to all older adults with heart disease.

studies.headline: New Oral Diabetes Pill Clears Heart-Safety Hurdle in Large Trial of Older Adults
studies.the_study: In the ACHIEVE-4 trial, 2,749 adults with type 2 diabetes (mean age 63) and established cardiovascular or chronic kidney disease were randomly assigned to once-daily oral orforglipron — a pill version of a GLP-1 drug — or injected insulin glargine, and followed for a median of two years. Major cardiac events occurred in 4.2% of the orforglipron group versus 5.0% on insulin, meeting the trial's non-inferiority bar for cardiovascular safety. Serious low blood sugar was far less common with the pill (6.8% vs 19.2%), but gastrointestinal side effects were much more frequent (62.1% vs 14.2%).
studies.why_it_matters: For older adults with diabetes and heart disease who dread injections or have had dangerous hypoglycemia, a daily pill with demonstrated cardiovascular safety and much lower hypoglycemia risk could meaningfully change treatment options.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you take insulin and have had episodes of dangerously low blood sugar, it may be worth asking your doctor whether oral GLP-1 options could become appropriate for you — while understanding that nausea, vomiting, and other digestive side effects were the leading reason people in this trial stopped the drug.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For caregivers and senior living staff: an oral alternative would simplify daily diabetes routines and reduce the hypoglycemia monitoring burden, but the high rate of gastrointestinal side effects raises real concerns about appetite, hydration, and unintended weight loss in frail residents.
studies.caveats: Funded by Eli Lilly and Company, which manufactures the drug; several authors are company employees and shareholders and most others report industry consultancy fees. Open-label design (participants and clinicians knew the assignment); trial tested safety, not superiority, with a wide non-inferiority margin; median follow-up only two years; average age 63, so results in the oldest and frailest adults are less certain.

studies.headline: A History of Depression Tracks With Higher Heart and Metabolic Disease Risk 15 Years Later
studies.the_study: Dutch researchers followed 1,858 adults from the NESDA cohort — people with a lifetime history of major depression plus non-depressed comparison participants, none of whom had cardiometabolic disease at the start — for 15 years. Those with major depressive disorder were about 65% more likely to develop cardiometabolic disease. Notably, no particular depression symptom pattern stood out: fatigue- and appetite-related 'atypical' symptoms, anhedonia, and classic symptoms all carried broadly similar risk.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests depression of any flavor, not just a particular subtype, belongs on the list of things that warrant closer attention to blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood sugar over the long haul.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you've lived with depression at any point, consider mentioning that history when discussing heart health with your doctor, and don't skip routine checks of blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood sugar — this study found elevated cardiometabolic risk persisting across 15 years.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For families and care staff: a resident's mental health history is relevant medical information for physical health monitoring, not a separate file. Flagging a depression history during care planning may support more vigilant cardiometabolic screening.
studies.caveats: Observational design cannot establish that depression causes cardiometabolic disease; outcomes relied partly on self-report and medication records; Dutch cohort recruited in adulthood rather than specifically older age, so generalization to seniors is indirect; several authors report consultancy or speaker fees from pharmaceutical companies including Novo Nordisk and Johnson & Johnson.

studies.headline: Financial Strain and Discrimination Show Up in the Blood of Older Black Adults With Heart Disease
studies.the_study: Researchers measured 92 inflammatory proteins in blood samples from 642 urban-dwelling older Black adults (mean age 75) and compared them against reported financial burden, perceived stress, and experiences of discrimination. Psychosocial stress alone showed little independent link to inflammation — but among participants who already had heart disease, financial burden and discrimination were associated with altered levels of 11 to 20 inflammatory proteins. Hypertension was present in 80% of the group and diabetes in 25%.
studies.why_it_matters: It offers biological evidence that money worries and experiences of unfair treatment may compound inflammation specifically in older adults who already carry a heart disease burden — a group for whom stress is often treated as a soft, secondary concern.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you're managing heart disease, financial pressure and experiences of discrimination are not just emotional strains to tough out — this research suggests they may interact with your physical health. It's reasonable to raise money worries and stress with your care team and ask about social work or benefits counseling.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For senior living operators and care teams: connecting residents to benefits assistance, financial counseling, and culturally responsive care may be more than a quality-of-life amenity for those with existing cardiovascular disease. Screening for financial strain could belong alongside clinical screening.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional observational analysis — cannot establish that stress causes inflammation or determine which came first; exploratory statistical approach with a lenient false discovery threshold (q<0.10) and many comparisons; stressors were self-reported; participants were predominantly women (19.3% men) and highly educated urban residents, limiting generalization; authors explicitly call for replication.

studies.headline: Depression Raises Heart Disease and Death Risk in People With Type 2 Diabetes — and Blood Sugar Isn't the Reason
studies.the_study: Researchers tracked 571,129 Chinese adults with type 2 diabetes (mean age 60, 66% women) who attended structured diabetes assessments in Hong Kong between 2000 and 2024, none of whom had cardiovascular disease at the start. The 7.5% who had depression — identified by diagnostic codes or antidepressant prescriptions — had a 21% higher risk of developing cardiovascular disease and a 30% higher risk of dying from any cause, plus more hospital admissions and longer stays. Mediation analysis of eight cardiometabolic risk factors found that blood sugar, cholesterol, blood pressure and similar measures explained very little of the excess risk; the effect of depression appeared to be largely direct.
studies.why_it_matters: For the millions of older adults living with type 2 diabetes, this suggests that mood is not a separate issue from heart health — and that treating only the numbers on a lab report may miss a meaningful driver of cardiovascular risk and early death.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you have type 2 diabetes and have been feeling persistently low, withdrawn or hopeless, it's worth raising at your next diabetes appointment rather than waiting for a separate mental health visit — ask whether depression screening is part of your routine diabetes care.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For care teams and senior living staff, this is an argument for integrated care: depression screening belongs inside the diabetes clinic workflow, and a resident's declining mood may warrant the same urgency as a rising HbA1c, given the associated hospitalization burden.
studies.caveats: Observational cohort — cannot prove depression causes cardiovascular events; depression was identified from diagnostic codes and antidepressant prescriptions, so milder or untreated cases were likely missed; single health system in Hong Kong and findings may not generalize to other populations; multiple authors report extensive grants and honoraria from pharmaceutical companies including AstraZeneca, Boehringer Ingelheim, Novo Nordisk and Sanofi.

studies.headline: A Pro-Inflammatory Diet Was Linked to a 64% Higher Stroke Risk in a Large Asian Cohort
studies.the_study: Investigators scored the inflammatory potential of the diets of 10,640 Chinese, Malay and Indian adults aged 21–65 in Singapore's Multi-Ethnic Cohort using a validated food-frequency questionnaire, then linked participants to national registries over roughly 887,500 person-years. Those eating the most pro-inflammatory diets had a 64% higher risk of nonfatal stroke than those eating the least inflammatory diets, and the association held after accounting for body mass index. No significant link was found for heart attack, cardiovascular death, cancer incidence or cancer death, and the stroke association was stronger among smokers.
studies.why_it_matters: Stroke is a leading cause of disability in later life, and this adds evidence that the overall inflammatory character of a dietary pattern — not just salt or saturated fat — may matter for stroke prevention.
studies.story_angle_primary: If stroke prevention is on your mind, consider the overall pattern of what you eat rather than single nutrients: diets weighted toward vegetables, fruit, whole grains, fish and tea score as less inflammatory, and the link appeared strongest in people who smoke — one more reason to ask for help quitting.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Dining program directors and family cooks can use this as support for menu patterns built around anti-inflammatory staples, though the study tested a score, not a specific meal plan, so there's no prescriptive menu to copy.
studies.caveats: Observational design — cannot establish causation; diet measured once by self-reported food-frequency questionnaire; cohort recruited at ages 21–65, so findings are not specific to the oldest adults; the score was adapted for Asian diets and may not transfer directly to Western eating patterns; relatively modest event counts for some outcomes.

studies.headline: Getting Up to Urinate at Night May Flag Higher Heart Risk in Men With Sleep Apnea
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed 603 patients aged 30–74 with untreated obstructive sleep apnea from the Sydney Sleep Biobank (67.5% male, mean age 54), comparing Framingham Risk Scores between those who reported nocturia disturbing their sleep three or more times a week and those who reported it less often. Just over half reported significant nocturia, and it was associated with high cardiovascular risk (odds ratio 1.72 after adjusting for confounders). The association held in men but was not seen in women.
studies.why_it_matters: Frequent nighttime urination is often dismissed as a normal nuisance of aging or a prostate issue, but in men with sleep apnea it may be a simple, free signal of elevated cardiovascular risk that warrants a closer look.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you're waking up several times a night to urinate and you snore, gasp or have been told you may have sleep apnea, mention both symptoms together to your doctor and ask whether a cardiovascular risk assessment is appropriate — nocturia isn't always just a bladder or prostate matter.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Night staff and family caregivers are often the first to notice repeated nighttime bathroom trips; documenting frequency alongside snoring or witnessed breathing pauses gives clinicians a more useful picture than either observation alone.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional analysis of a clinical biobank — shows association, not prediction or causation; nocturia was self-reported via a single sleep-quality questionnaire item; sleep-clinic patients skew male and heavier (mean BMI 32) and may not represent older adults generally; no women-specific signal found; authors note prospective studies are needed.

studies.headline: Long-Term Lithium Use Was Linked to Less Artery Calcification in People With Bipolar Disorder
studies.the_study: Researchers reviewed baseline and roughly 10-year follow-up chest X-rays from 177 patients with bipolar disorder, grouping them by whether they had been treated with lithium, and scored aortic and coronary artery calcification. Lithium treatment was independently associated with much lower odds of both aortic calcification (adjusted odds ratio 0.11) and coronary calcification (0.19). More frequent mood episodes were linked to more aortic calcification, as were age and diabetes.
studies.why_it_matters: People with bipolar disorder carry elevated cardiovascular risk, and this raises the possibility that a long-standing mood stabilizer may not add to that risk — a relevant consideration for older adults weighing decades of medication use.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you or a family member takes lithium long-term, this is reassuring context rather than a reason to change anything — but it is a good prompt to ask your prescriber how your heart and kidney health are being monitored alongside your lithium levels.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For clinicians and care staff supporting older adults with serious mental illness, the finding that greater mood-episode burden tracked with arterial calcification reinforces that psychiatric stability and cardiovascular care are intertwined, not parallel tracks.
studies.caveats: Small retrospective cohort (N=177), single-population sample from China, observational design that cannot establish causation; calcification assessed from chest X-rays rather than CT; patients who tolerate lithium long-term may be systematically healthier (confounding by indication); prediction models described by the authors themselves as exploratory.

studies.headline: Which Combinations of Chronic Conditions Carry the Highest Risk? A 16,000-Person Study Maps Them Out
studies.journal: J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed data from 16,095 Australians aged 70 and older in the ASPREE trial, none of whom had dementia or cardiovascular disease at the start, and used statistical clustering to see how 15 chronic conditions grouped together. Nearly 9 in 10 participants already had two or more conditions, and five distinct clusters emerged — the largest being hypertension plus high cholesterol (52%). Over a median follow-up of nearly 11 years, 4,217 people died; the cluster combining frailty, depressive symptoms and osteoporosis raised death risk by roughly 56% in men and 68% in women, and clusters involving gout, kidney disease and anemia raised risk by 63% in men and 96% in women.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests the particular mix of conditions an older person carries may matter more than the simple count, and that some combinations — especially frailty with low mood and bone loss — flag substantially elevated risk that might otherwise be dismissed as ordinary aging.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you are managing several conditions at once, it may be worth asking your doctor to look at them as a package rather than one appointment at a time — particularly if frailty, low mood and osteoporosis, or gout and kidney problems, appear together on your chart. These patterns were linked to higher mortality in this study, though it cannot prove the combinations themselves caused the deaths.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For care teams and senior living staff, the findings argue for recognizing frailty and depressive symptoms as red flags of equal weight to the more familiar metabolic diagnoses, and for noting that risky clusters differed between men and women — the same checklist may not serve both residents equally.
studies.caveats: Observational secondary analysis of a clinical trial cohort — cannot establish causation; participants were relatively healthy volunteers aged 70+ without baseline dementia or cardiovascular disease, so findings may not generalize to frailer or sicker populations; authors describe results as hypothesis-generating. Several investigators report grants and honoraria from government agencies, AARP, Optum Labs and others.

studies.headline: Heart Risk Scores May Also Forecast How Fast Memory Slips
studies.the_study: In Project FRONTIER, a rural West Texas cohort, researchers followed 383 adults aged 40 and older (average age 58, 76% women, 60% Hispanic) who had no cardiovascular disease at baseline and completed cognitive testing at two visits a median of three years apart. Using the American Heart Association's PREVENT equations to calculate 10-year heart disease risk, they found that each 10 percentage points of higher cardiovascular risk was associated with roughly 1.2 extra points of annual decline on a global cognitive battery. The sharpest declines showed up in attention and delayed memory, with corroborating changes on clock drawing and a timed connect-the-dots test.
studies.why_it_matters: It reinforces that the numbers driving heart risk — blood pressure, cholesterol, blood sugar, smoking — travel with brain health, and that a standard cardiovascular risk score may double as an early signal about cognitive trajectory.
studies.story_angle_primary: Next time your clinician calculates your 10-year heart risk, you can reasonably ask what that number might mean for your thinking and memory over the coming years — and treat blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar management as brain care as well as heart care. This study shows an association, not proof that lowering risk scores preserves cognition.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For families and care professionals in rural and underserved communities, where specialist memory services are scarce, the study suggests existing cardiovascular risk data already in the chart could help identify who warrants closer cognitive monitoring.
studies.caveats: Observational design — cannot establish causation; relatively small sample (N=383) from a single rural region with a largely female and Hispanic makeup, which may limit generalizability; short median follow-up of about three years with only two assessment points; participants were middle-aged on average rather than exclusively older adults.

studies.headline: An Eye Scan May Hint at Future Depression — and, in People Already Depressed, Heart Disease
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed retinal photographs from 43,445 UK Biobank participants, using automated software to measure the width, density and twistiness of blood vessels at the back of the eye, then tracked health outcomes for a median of 11.3 years. Among the 40,905 people without depression at the start, wider retinal veins were associated with a 25% to 31% higher risk of developing depression. Among 1,507 people who already had depression and no chronic disease, more tortuous retinal vessels were associated with roughly double the risk of later cardiovascular disease.
studies.why_it_matters: A routine, painless eye photograph — already taken at many optometry visits — may eventually carry information about mental health and heart risk, which is especially relevant for older adults whose depression often goes unrecognized and whose cardiovascular risk compounds it.
studies.story_angle_primary: This is early-stage research, so there is no retinal depression test to ask for yet — but it is one more reason to keep regular eye exams on your calendar, since the images taken there are becoming a window into more than vision.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For clinicians and senior living health teams, the stronger practical takeaway is the one already established in the data: older adults living with depression carry measurably elevated cardiovascular risk, which argues for active heart-health screening rather than treating mood and heart as separate lanes.
studies.caveats: Observational cohort — cannot establish causation; UK Biobank volunteers are healthier and less diverse than the general population; depression outcomes relied on registry and questionnaire definitions; the chronic disease analysis rested on a much smaller subgroup (n=1,507); retinal measures were derived by automated software requiring further validation.

studies.headline: Optimistic Older Adults Get Depressed Less Often — But Not Because Hard Times Hit Them Any Softer
studies.the_study: Drawing on 10,791 participants aged 70 and over in the ASPREE Longitudinal Study of Older Persons — all free of depression, dementia, cardiovascular disease and disabling impairment at baseline — researchers measured dispositional optimism and pessimism and tracked new depression over a median 3.5 years. Optimism was associated with modestly lower depression risk and pessimism with higher risk, even after adjusting for lifestyle, medical factors and a genetic risk score for depression. But contrary to the prevailing theory, optimism did not blunt the impact of stressful life events: stressors raised depression risk by about the same amount regardless of a person's outlook.
studies.why_it_matters: It tempers the popular idea that a positive attitude buffers seniors against bereavement, illness or financial shock, and suggests that practical support after a stressful event matters for everyone, including the people who seem temperamentally upbeat.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you consider yourself a glass-half-full person, this research suggests you are not immune after a hard loss or health scare — so take low mood seriously and seek help, rather than assuming your usual outlook will carry you through.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For families and senior living staff, this is a caution against triaging emotional support by personality: the cheerful resident who has just lost a spouse or received a serious diagnosis needs the same proactive check-ins as anyone else.
studies.caveats: Observational cohort — cannot establish causation; depression was defined by a self-report screening scale (CES-D ≥8) rather than clinical diagnosis, and stressors were self-reported; participants were relatively healthy, independent Australians aged 70+ free of major disease at baseline, so results may not generalize to frailer or already-depressed older adults; median follow-up of 3.5 years is relatively short.

studies.headline: Calcium scans add only modest precision to the new heart-risk calculator — but help most in the middle
studies.the_study: Researchers followed 6,098 adults aged 45 to 79 without known cardiovascular disease in the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (mean age 61, 52% female) for 10 years, during which 366 had a heart attack, stroke, or other atherosclerotic event. They tested whether adding a coronary artery calcium (CAC) score to the new PREVENT risk equations improved prediction. Overall discrimination improved only slightly (C statistic rose from 0.73 by 0.02), but among people in the 'borderline' risk band, 10-year event rates ranged from 1.9% with a calcium score of zero to 14.3% with a score of 300 or higher.
studies.why_it_matters: Calcium scans are increasingly marketed directly to older adults, and this study clarifies who actually gains useful information: those whose estimated risk sits in the gray zone where a statin decision could go either way.
studies.story_angle_primary: If your doctor has estimated your 10-year heart risk in the borderline-to-intermediate range and you are undecided about starting a statin, it's reasonable to ask whether a coronary calcium scan would sharpen the picture — and equally reasonable to ask whether it would change anything if your risk is already clearly low or clearly high.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For senior living health teams and family advocates: this is a useful counterweight to walk-in 'heart scan' advertising. The test's value is conditional on where a resident's baseline risk already sits, so the first question is whether a formal PREVENT risk estimate has even been calculated.
studies.caveats: Observational cohort — it measures prediction accuracy, not whether scanning improves outcomes. Several authors report personal fees or grants from imaging and pharmaceutical companies (including Heartflow, Nanox AI, Amgen, Novartis, Eli Lilly). Participants were 45-79, so findings may not extend to the oldest old.

studies.headline: Three in four older adults with high blood pressure in one rural county weren't at goal
studies.journal: J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci
studies.the_study: Investigators analyzed annual wellness review data from 813 Medicare beneficiaries with diagnosed hypertension in rural Abbeville County, South Carolina (55.6% female, mean age 73.2). Using the 130/80 mmHg threshold, 76.3% had uncontrolled blood pressure whether or not they were on medication. Being overweight or obese roughly doubled the odds of uncontrolled pressure; unexpectedly, self-reported frequent physical activity was also linked to higher odds, which the authors flag as a sign that self-reported activity data may be unreliable.
studies.why_it_matters: Rural older adults already face higher cardiovascular death rates, and this real-world snapshot suggests that having a hypertension diagnosis and a prescription is far from the same thing as having blood pressure under control.
studies.story_angle_primary: Having a blood pressure prescription does not mean your numbers are where they should be. Consider checking at home between visits, bringing the readings to your next appointment, and asking directly: 'Am I at my target, and if not, what changes next?'
studies.story_angle_secondary: For caregivers and rural senior service providers: a 76% uncontrolled rate points to a systems gap, not individual failure. Home monitoring support, transportation to follow-up visits, and medication review are concrete places to intervene.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional and observational — causation cannot be inferred. Single rural county in South Carolina, so results may not generalize. Physical activity and other behaviors were self-reported, which the authors themselves identify as a likely source of the counterintuitive activity finding.

studies.headline: Women's heart disease in Europe looks different from men's — and pregnancy history is a bigger part of the story than assumed
studies.the_study: Using Global Burden of Disease 2023 data across 55 European Society of Cardiology member countries, researchers compared cardiovascular disease burden and risk factor exposure by sex from 1990 to 2023. Women accounted for 55% of cases and 50% of deaths — apparent parity that masked sharp differences in disease type: ischemic heart disease made up 21% of women's cardiovascular burden versus 38% of men's, while peripheral arterial disease contributed more in women. Maternal hypertensive disorders accounted for 25% of incident cardiovascular disease in women, and tobacco and alcohol exposure ran 10-20 percentage points higher in men while high body mass index and low physical activity ran 5-15 points higher in women.
studies.why_it_matters: Heart disease prevention advice built around the classic male pattern of ischemic heart disease may miss conditions that matter more for women, including peripheral arterial disease and the long shadow cast by pregnancy-related high blood pressure decades earlier.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you are a woman, your pregnancy history is cardiovascular history. Make sure any episode of high blood pressure or preeclampsia during pregnancy — even 40 years ago — is in your current medical record, and ask about leg symptoms like pain when walking, not just chest symptoms.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For clinicians and care staff taking histories from older women: obstetric history and peripheral arterial symptoms deserve a place alongside the standard cholesterol-and-smoking checklist, and country-of-origin matters given up to 25-fold differences in premature cardiovascular mortality across Europe.
studies.caveats: Modeled population-level estimates from the Global Burden of Disease study, not individual patient data; ecological design cannot establish causation. European region only, so patterns may not transfer to other populations. Data quality varies substantially between countries.

studies.headline: Menopause before 45 flagged higher death risk after a heart attack in a five-year registry
studies.the_study: Croatian researchers tracked 728 women aged 60 or younger hospitalized with acute coronary syndrome across multiple centers between 2020 and 2025, with a median follow-up of 3.52 years. Of these, 124 had gone through menopause before age 45. Early menopause was associated with higher rates of major adverse cardiovascular events (21.1% vs 13.3%) and death (8.9% vs 4.6%), with an adjusted hazard ratio of 2.57 for death; the associations weakened in extended models accounting for prior vascular disease, surgical menopause, and hormone therapy.
studies.why_it_matters: Age at menopause is rarely recorded in cardiology charts, yet this registry suggests it may mark a group of women who need closer follow-up after a heart event.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you went through menopause before 45, that's worth mentioning to your cardiologist — especially after a heart attack or stent. It is not a reason for alarm, but it is information that belongs in your record and may argue for tighter follow-up.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For families and care coordinators helping assemble a medical history: reproductive milestones are routinely left out of cardiac records. Adding age at menopause and whether it was surgical takes one line and may change how aggressively secondary prevention is pursued.
studies.caveats: Observational registry analysis — the authors explicitly state causality cannot be inferred. Menopausal age came from clinical history fields and may be imprecise. Associations attenuated when additional variables were added, suggesting confounding. Single-country (Croatian) cohort of women 60 and under, so findings may not generalize to older women or other health systems.

studies.headline: People over 80 are dying less — and living longer with disability
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed Global Burden of Disease 2023 data from 1990 to 2023 for adults aged 80 and older across 10 selected countries, where the population in this age group grew from 31.8 million to 103.8 million. Years of life lost fell in every country (median -31.3%) while years lived with disability rose in six, pushing the disabling share of total health loss from a median of 19.0% to 25.9%. Cardiovascular disease's share of burden dropped sharply, from 42.3% to 28.6%, while cancer and neurological conditions grew.
studies.why_it_matters: The dominant health challenge in the oldest age group is shifting away from fatal heart disease and toward conditions that erode function and independence — which is exactly what long-term care and senior living are built to address.
studies.story_angle_primary: The gains against heart disease mean you are more likely than previous generations to reach 85 or 90. That makes planning for function — mobility, cognition, vision, hearing, and the home environment — at least as important as managing your cholesterol numbers.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For senior living operators and care planners: the burden mix in the 80-plus population is changing, with neurological and cancer-related needs growing while cardiovascular deaths recede. Staffing, programming, and rehabilitation capacity built around a 1990s disease profile may be increasingly mismatched to residents' actual needs.
studies.caveats: Modeled population-level estimates, not individual data; the authors caution the findings do not establish individual-level expansion or compression of morbidity. Only 10 purposively selected countries, limiting generalizability. Underlying Global Burden of Disease estimates vary in quality by country and era.

studies.headline: Your Heart Risk Score May Also Be a Window Into Your Brain
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed brain scans and cognitive testing from 1,626 participants in the Health and Aging Brain Study-Health Disparities (HABS-HD), a racially and ethnically diverse cohort of adults who had no diagnosed cardiovascular disease or dementia. They calculated each person's standard 10-year risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (heart attack and stroke) and compared it with PET and MRI markers of amyloid, tau, brain shrinkage, and white matter damage. Higher 10-year heart risk tracked with more amyloid and tau signal, thinner cortex, smaller hippocampal volume, more white matter damage, and lower scores in memory, executive function, processing speed, and language — even after accounting for APOE ε4 status and amyloid burden.
studies.why_it_matters: The same numbers your doctor uses to decide about blood pressure and cholesterol treatment appear to mark brain health burden too, reinforcing that cardiovascular care and brain care are not separate projects.
studies.story_angle_primary: At your next visit, you can ask what your 10-year cardiovascular risk score is and discuss how the modifiable pieces — blood pressure, cholesterol, smoking, diabetes — are being managed; this study can't prove lowering that score protects your memory, but it shows heart risk and brain changes travel together.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For families and care staff: when a resident or relative has a heavy cardiovascular risk profile, it may be worth watching for subtle changes in word-finding, planning, or processing speed rather than assuming cognitive concerns are a separate issue from the heart chart.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional design — cannot establish causation or which came first; associations with amyloid and tau were modest and only statistically significant among amyloid-negative participants; findings come from a specific health-disparities cohort and may not generalize to all populations.

studies.headline: More Than a Third of Hispanic/Latino Adults With Diabetes Had Retinopathy — and Blood Pressure Was a Key Culprit
studies.the_study: In SOL Ojos, an eye study embedded in the large Hispanic Community Health Study/Study of Latinos, researchers performed standardized eye exams with centrally graded ultra-widefield retinal imaging on 1,224 adults aged 40 and older with diabetes (mean age 62.7). Age-standardized prevalence of any diabetic retinopathy was 34.7%, higher in men (41.8%) than women (27.2%), and ranged widely by heritage group — from about 14% to 55% — with the highest estimates among Cuban participants. Cardiovascular risk factors clustered heavily (over 40% of men had four or more), and hypertension was independently associated with roughly triple the odds of any retinopathy and nearly triple the odds of vision-threatening disease.
studies.why_it_matters: Vision loss from diabetes is largely preventable with timely screening and blood pressure control, and these numbers show how common — and how unevenly distributed — the problem is among older Hispanic/Latino adults.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you have diabetes, ask whether you are up to date on a dilated or retinal-imaging eye exam, and treat your blood pressure numbers as an eye issue as well as a heart issue — hypertension was one of the strongest factors linked to sight-threatening retinopathy here.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For families and senior living staff: eye exams are frequently the first appointment to slip when transportation or scheduling gets hard; building retinal screening into the routine care calendar for residents with diabetes is a concrete, low-cost way to protect independence.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional observational study — cannot establish causation; cumulative cardiovascular risk burden was not significantly associated with vision-threatening disease overall; some heritage-group estimates had very wide confidence intervals; participants were drawn from Chicago and Miami only.

studies.headline: The Circulation Problem in Your Legs That Deserves as Much Attention as Your Heart
studies.the_study: In the first of a three-part clinical series, an international group of vascular specialists synthesizes current evidence on lower-extremity peripheral arterial disease (PAD) — clogged arteries in the legs. They report that PAD is frequently silent for years or decades and is typically caught only at an advanced stage, at which point five-year mortality runs between 30% and 50%, exceeding outcomes for severe cancer and acute heart attack. The authors argue PAD is systematically underdiagnosed, under-researched, and undertreated relative to heart and stroke disease, compounded by poor adherence to preventive medication and lifestyle care.
studies.why_it_matters: PAD is common in older adults and its warning signs — leg pain with walking, slow-healing foot sores, cold or discolored feet — are easy to dismiss as normal aging, yet late diagnosis carries a worse prognosis than many cancers.
studies.story_angle_primary: If walking a block brings on cramping calf or thigh pain that eases when you stop, or if a foot sore isn't healing, raise it specifically with your doctor and ask whether an ankle-brachial index test is appropriate — don't file it under 'getting older.'
studies.story_angle_secondary: For caregivers and senior living professionals: routine foot checks and noticing when a resident quietly shortens their walking distance can surface PAD long before it becomes limb-threatening; the series also highlights how often preventive medications for PAD go unfilled or unused.
studies.caveats: This is a narrative clinical review rather than new primary data; several authors report consulting fees, honoraria, or travel funding from device and pharmaceutical companies including Bayer, Novo Nordisk, AstraZeneca, Abbott, and Gore Medical.

studies.headline: The ECG Recorded During Your Sleep Study May Predict Heart Trouble a Decade Out
studies.the_study: Researchers trained a deep learning model on single-lead electrocardiogram traces — a signal routinely recorded during overnight sleep studies but usually ignored — from 15,809 patients at Massachusetts General Hospital, then tested it in two independent hospital cohorts (9,810 and 12,576 patients). The model's output predicted 10-year risk of atrial fibrillation, stroke, heart failure, heart attack, and death, even after adjusting for age, sex, BMI, smoking, hypertension, diabetes, and detailed sleep measures like apnea severity. A one-standard-deviation higher score was linked to roughly double to triple the hazard of atrial fibrillation and 65–82% higher risk of death.
studies.why_it_matters: Millions of older adults undergo sleep studies for apnea or insomnia; this suggests that data already being collected could double as a free cardiovascular risk screen without any extra test, visit, or cost.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you have had or are scheduled for an overnight sleep study, it's reasonable to ask whether your heart rhythm data was reviewed — and to make sure your sleep results actually get communicated to the clinician managing your blood pressure and heart risk.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For care coordinators and families: sleep study results often sit in a silo. Closing the loop between the sleep center and the primary care or cardiology team is a practical care-navigation step this research makes more valuable.
studies.caveats: Retrospective analysis of hospital records with outcomes based on billing codes; the model was developed and tested in patients referred for sleep studies, who may not represent the general older population; prediction for heart attack was not significant in one validation cohort; no evidence yet that acting on the score improves outcomes.

studies.headline: Dirty Air Appears to Speed Up Biological Aging — and Cleaner Air May Partly Reverse It
studies.the_study: This review synthesizes epidemiological and laboratory evidence linking air pollution — especially fine and ultrafine particulates, traffic exhaust, and household cooking and heating smoke — to measures of biological aging. The authors report that composite biological-age indices (Klemera-Doubal biological age, PhenoAge) and frailty scores show the most consistent associations with pollution exposure, while epigenetic clock findings remain inconclusive. Causal mediation analyses across independent cohorts suggest accelerated biological aging is one pathway connecting pollution to cardiovascular disease, kidney disease, and neuropsychiatric disorders; notably, air quality improvements and switches to clean cooking fuels partially reversed pollution-associated aging acceleration.
studies.why_it_matters: Frailty and cardiovascular risk in later life may be shaped partly by the air around you, and the evidence that improvements help suggests exposure reduction is worth taking seriously even at older ages.
studies.story_angle_primary: On high-pollution days, you can shift walks and errands away from busy roads and peak traffic hours, consider indoor air filtration, and make sure gas stoves and wood or kerosene heating are well-ventilated — small exposure reductions appear to matter for cardiovascular and frailty outcomes.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For senior living operators and family caregivers: siting outdoor activity away from traffic corridors, tracking local air quality alerts for residents with heart or lung disease, and investing in building filtration are concrete operational responses to this evidence base.
studies.caveats: Narrative review of observational and mechanistic studies, not new primary data; causation is not firmly established; the authors note underrepresentation of household air pollution and low-income settings and a shortage of longitudinal multimarker designs.

fact_check.headline: Trouble Reading Small Print May Quietly Undermine Heart Patients' Recovery
fact_check.notes: Sample size, prevalence, odds ratio and hazard ratio all match the abstract; framing is appropriately associational and caveats cover the self-report and generalizability limits.

fact_check.headline: New Oral Diabetes Pill Clears Heart-Safety Hurdle in Large Trial of Older Adults
fact_check.notes: Trial design, N, mean age, median follow-up, MACE-4 rates, hypoglycemia and GI adverse-event rates all match; Eli Lilly funding and employee authorship are disclosed in Caveats.

fact_check.headline: A History of Depression Tracks With Higher Heart and Metabolic Disease Risk 15 Years Later
fact_check.notes: N, cohort, follow-up and HR 1.65 are correct; the 'no symptom pattern stood out' line slightly flattens the abstract's finding that atypical energy-related symptoms were the only profile significantly associated in continuous analyses and the only one linked to diabetes.

issues.label: Symptom-profile nuance flattened
issues.as_written: Notably, no particular depression symptom pattern stood out: fatigue- and appetite-related 'atypical' symptoms, anhedonia, and classic symptoms all carried broadly similar risk.
issues.abstract_says: In continuous analyses, only AES and depression severity were significantly associated with CMD incidence, though effect sizes were comparable across symptom profiles... All profiles were associated with cardiovascular disease incidence, but only AES was associated with diabetes incidence.
issues.problem: The abstract does report one distinguishing result — atypical energy-related symptoms were the only profile significantly associated in continuous analyses and the only one linked to incident diabetes — which the digest omits.
issues.suggested_fix: Add a clause such as 'although atypical, fatigue-related symptoms were the only profile linked specifically to new diabetes.'

fact_check.headline: Financial Strain and Discrimination Show Up in the Blood of Older Black Adults With Heart Disease
fact_check.notes: Protein count, N, mean age, hypertension and diabetes prevalences, and the 11–20 protein interaction counts all match. The digest omits that only 6.8% of the sample had heart disease, so the key interaction rests on a very small subgroup, though the Caveats do flag the exploratory, replication-needed nature of the work.

issues.label: Size of the heart-disease subgroup not reported
issues.as_written: but among participants who already had heart disease, financial burden and discrimination were associated with altered levels of 11 to 20 inflammatory proteins
issues.abstract_says: Cardiovascular burden included BMI (mean = 30.6, SD = 6.4 kg/m2), hypertension (80.1%), type 2 diabetes (25.1%), and heart disease (6.8%).
issues.problem: Only about 6.8% of the 642 participants (roughly 44 people) had heart disease, so the headline interaction is based on a very small subgroup — context a reader needs to judge the strength of the finding.
issues.suggested_fix: Note that heart disease was present in just 6.8% of participants, making that subgroup small.

fact_check.headline: Depression Raises Heart Disease and Death Risk in People With Type 2 Diabetes — and Blood Sugar Isn't the Reason
fact_check.notes: N, cohort period, 7.5% depression prevalence, HRs of 1.21 and 1.30, and the mediation conclusion are all accurately reported; the headline verb 'Raises' is causal language for an observational cohort, and the null finding for end-stage kidney disease is omitted.

issues.label: Causal verb in headline
issues.as_written: Depression Raises Heart Disease and Death Risk in People With Type 2 Diabetes — and Blood Sugar Isn't the Reason
issues.abstract_says: Depression is associated with greater risks for incident cardiovascular disease and all-cause death in people with type 2 diabetes.
issues.problem: 'Raises' asserts causation from an observational cohort; the body text and Caveats correctly say 'associated' and note causation cannot be proven, so the headline overstates relative to the rest of the item.
issues.suggested_fix: Change to 'Depression Is Linked to Higher Heart Disease and Death Risk in People With Type 2 Diabetes.'

issues.label: Null kidney outcome omitted
issues.as_written: had a 21% higher risk of developing cardiovascular disease and a 30% higher risk of dying from any cause, plus more hospital admissions and longer stays
issues.problem: The digest reports only the positive outcomes; the abstract also reports no association with end-stage kidney disease, which bounds the finding.
issues.suggested_fix: Add that depression was not associated with end-stage kidney disease.

fact_check.headline: A Pro-Inflammatory Diet Was Linked to a 64% Higher Stroke Risk in a Large Asian Cohort
fact_check.notes: N, age range, person-years, HR 1.64 for nonfatal stroke, BMI adjustment, null findings for other outcomes and the smoking interaction all match. One illustrative detail about which foods score as less inflammatory is not in the abstract.

issues.label: Food examples not in the abstract
issues.as_written: diets weighted toward vegetables, fruit, whole grains, fish and tea score as less inflammatory
issues.abstract_says: The EDIP-A score was calculated using a validated food-frequency questionnaire.
issues.problem: The abstract does not list the component foods of the EDIP-A score, so the specific food examples are unverifiable from abstract only.
issues.suggested_fix: Attribute the food examples to the EDIP-A score's published components or drop the specifics.

fact_check.headline: Getting Up to Urinate at Night May Flag Higher Heart Risk in Men With Sleep Apnea
fact_check.notes: N, age range, sex distribution, mean age and BMI, 51% nocturia prevalence, adjusted OR 1.72 and the men-only sex-stratified result all match; framing stays associational and caveats mirror the authors' call for prospective work.

fact_check.headline: Long-Term Lithium Use Was Linked to Less Artery Calcification in People With Bipolar Disorder
fact_check.notes: N=177, ~10-year follow-up chest radiographs, adjusted ORs of 0.11 and 0.19, and the mood-episode/age/diabetes associations all match; the exploratory nature of the prediction models is correctly flagged.

fact_check.headline: Which Combinations of Chronic Conditions Carry the Highest Risk? A 16,000-Person Study Maps Them Out
fact_check.notes: N, age criteria, 88.3% multimorbidity, five clusters, 52.1% largest cluster, 4,217 deaths over 10.85 years median and the sex-specific hazard ratios are all accurate; two small wording points — causal phrasing and merging of two differently named clusters.

issues.label: Causal phrasing for cluster mortality
issues.as_written: the cluster combining frailty, depressive symptoms and osteoporosis raised death risk by roughly 56% in men and 68% in women
issues.abstract_says: The frailty, depressive symptoms and osteoporosis cluster was associated with higher mortality in both sexes (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 1.56 ... in males; 1.68 ... in females).
issues.problem: 'Raised death risk' implies causation in a secondary observational analysis; the abstract uses 'associated with'. The story angle does add a disclaimer, but the body text states it causally.
issues.suggested_fix: Use 'was associated with roughly 56% higher mortality in men and 68% in women.'

issues.label: Two distinct clusters merged
issues.as_written: clusters involving gout, kidney disease and anemia raised risk by 63% in men and 96% in women
issues.abstract_says: Higher mortality was also observed for the metabolic, gout and kidney disease cluster in males (aHR 1.63 [1.47-1.81]) and the gout, anemia and kidney disease cluster in females (aHR 1.96 [1.74-2.21]).
issues.problem: The male and female clusters were differently composed (metabolic/gout/kidney in men; gout/anemia/kidney in women); the digest's single combined description blurs that distinction.
issues.suggested_fix: Name the two clusters separately, as the abstract does.

fact_check.headline: Heart Risk Scores May Also Forecast How Fast Memory Slips
fact_check.notes: N=383, mean age 57.7, 75.5% female, 59.8% Hispanic, median 3-year follow-up, the -1.22 RBANS points/year per 10% higher ASCVD risk, and the attention/delayed memory/CLOX/TMT-A findings all match; associational framing is maintained.

fact_check.headline: An Eye Scan May Hint at Future Depression — and, in People Already Depressed, Heart Disease
fact_check.notes: Cohort size, subgroup numbers, follow-up and hazard ratios all match the abstract; framing is appropriately associational.

fact_check.headline: Optimistic Older Adults Get Depressed Less Often — But Not Because Hard Times Hit Them Any Softer
fact_check.notes: N, cohort, follow-up, CES-D threshold, direction of effects and the null interaction with stressors all match the abstract.

fact_check.headline: Calcium scans add only modest precision to the new heart-risk calculator — but help most in the middle
fact_check.notes: Sample, event count, C statistic change and borderline-band event rates match; industry disclosures correctly carried into Caveats.

fact_check.headline: Three in four older adults with high blood pressure in one rural county weren't at goal
fact_check.notes: Prevalence, sample characteristics, odds ratios and the counterintuitive physical-activity finding are reported faithfully; the authors' call for objective measures supports the digest's interpretation.

fact_check.headline: Women's heart disease in Europe looks different from men's — and pregnancy history is a bigger part of the story than assumed
fact_check.notes: Core figures accurate; the 25-fold mortality disparity is women-specific in the abstract but presented as a general cross-Europe figure.

issues.label: 25-fold disparity not sex-specified
issues.as_written: country-of-origin matters given up to 25-fold differences in premature cardiovascular mortality across Europe
issues.abstract_says: even larger disparities in mortality and premature mortality (up to 25-fold in women)
issues.problem: The abstract attributes the up-to-25-fold premature mortality spread specifically to women; the digest presents it as a general cross-country figure, dropping the sex qualifier in a piece whose whole point is sex differences.
issues.suggested_fix: Write 'up to 25-fold differences in premature cardiovascular mortality among women across Europe'.

fact_check.headline: Menopause before 45 flagged higher death risk after a heart attack in a five-year registry
fact_check.notes: All numbers (728 women, 124 with early menopause, 21.1% vs 13.3%, 8.9% vs 4.6%, HR 2.57, attenuation in extended models) match. Headline shorthand slightly blurs the enrolment window versus follow-up and ACS versus heart attack.

issues.label: 'Five-year registry' and 'heart attack' shorthand
issues.as_written: Menopause before 45 flagged higher death risk after a heart attack in a five-year registry
issues.abstract_says: We analyzed a multicenter registry of women hospitalized with ACS from February 1, 2020 through February 28, 2025... median follow-up was 3.52 years
issues.problem: 'Five-year' refers to the enrolment window, not follow-up (median 3.52 years), and 'heart attack' narrows acute coronary syndrome, which also includes unstable angina. The body text is correct, but the headline could be misread.
issues.suggested_fix: Consider 'in a multicentre registry of women with acute coronary syndrome followed about 3.5 years'.

fact_check.headline: People over 80 are dying less — and living longer with disability
fact_check.notes: Population growth, YLL/YLD trends, disabling burden ratio and cause shares are reproduced accurately, but the headline and 'Why it matters' lean further toward morbidity expansion and non-fatal dominance than the abstract allows.

issues.label: Overstates the shift away from fatal burden
issues.as_written: The dominant health challenge in the oldest age group is shifting away from fatal heart disease and toward conditions that erode function and independence
issues.abstract_says: health loss at ages ≥80 years shifted toward a larger disabling share while fatal burden remained dominant... no country reached a YLD-over-YLL crossover. Mean cardiovascular-disease share decreased from 42.3% to 28.6%
issues.problem: The abstract stresses that fatal burden remained dominant and that no country crossed over to disability-dominated health loss; cardiovascular disease still holds the largest cause share. The digest frames the shift as having already changed which challenge dominates.
issues.suggested_fix: Say the disabling share of health loss is growing while fatal burden still dominates, and note cardiovascular disease remains the largest single cause share at 28.6%.

issues.label: 'Living longer with disability' is an individual-level claim
issues.as_written: People over 80 are dying less — and living longer with disability
issues.abstract_says: The findings... do not by themselves establish individual-level expansion or compression of morbidity
issues.problem: The headline states individual-level morbidity expansion, which the authors explicitly say their population-rate data cannot establish; the Caveats note this, so the headline contradicts the digest's own caveat.
issues.suggested_fix: Reframe as 'Disability makes up a growing share of health loss after 80' to stay at the population level.

fact_check.headline: Your Heart Risk Score May Also Be a Window Into Your Brain
fact_check.notes: Sample size, cohort description, biomarker and cognitive findings, adjustment set, and the amyloid-negative-only caveat all match the abstract.

fact_check.headline: More Than a Third of Hispanic/Latino Adults With Diabetes Had Retinopathy — and Blood Pressure Was a Key Culprit
fact_check.notes: Prevalence figures and odds ratios are accurate; the heritage-group range quoted is the male-specific range, and the 'preventable' framing goes beyond this cross-sectional study.

issues.label: Heritage-group range is men-only
issues.as_written: ranged widely by heritage group — from about 14% to 55%
issues.abstract_says: Any DR ranged across Hispanic/Latino backgrounds from 13.9%... to 55.4%... in men and 15.3%... to 39.2%... in women
issues.problem: The 14%-55% span is the range among men; among women the range was narrower (15.3%-39.2%). Presenting it without the sex qualifier overstates the spread for the sample as a whole.
issues.suggested_fix: Specify 'from about 14% to 55% among men (15% to 39% among women)'.

issues.label: Preventability claim not from this study
issues.as_written: Vision loss from diabetes is largely preventable with timely screening and blood pressure control
issues.abstract_says: Cross-sectional analysis... Hypertension was associated with DR outcomes, particularly VTDR... support longitudinal evaluation of cardiometabolic risk and DR outcomes
issues.problem: The cross-sectional design shows association only; the claim that blood pressure control prevents vision loss is outside background knowledge drawn from this paper and reads as a finding of it.
issues.suggested_fix: Attribute the preventability point to existing guidelines, e.g. 'screening and blood pressure control are standard prevention advice, and these numbers show how common the problem is'.

issues.label: Population described as 'older' adults
issues.as_written: how unevenly distributed — the problem is among older Hispanic/Latino adults
issues.abstract_says: Adults aged ≥40 years... mean age, 62.7 years
issues.problem: The sample is adults 40 and older, not specifically older adults; framing the prevalence as an older-adult statistic slightly overgeneralizes to the digest's primary audience.
issues.suggested_fix: Say 'among Hispanic/Latino adults aged 40 and over'.

fact_check.headline: The Circulation Problem in Your Legs That Deserves as Much Attention as Your Heart
fact_check.notes: Correctly identified as paper 1 of a three-part Lancet clinical Series; mortality range, underdiagnosis argument and author conflicts all match the abstract.

fact_check.headline: The ECG Recorded During Your Sleep Study May Predict Heart Trouble a Decade Out
fact_check.notes: Sample sizes, cohorts, adjustments and hazard ratios all match. Two small issues: the model combined ECG with sleep-stage data (not ECG alone), and the "free cardiovascular risk screen" framing overstates readiness of an unvalidated research tool.

issues.label: Model input described incompletely
issues.as_written: Researchers trained a deep learning model on single-lead electrocardiogram traces — a signal routinely recorded during overnight sleep studies but usually ignored — from 15,809 patients at Massachusetts General Hospital
issues.abstract_says: We applied a deep residual neural network with attention to single-lead ECGs from PSG, combined with sleep stage data, to predict 10-year risk... The network, trained for arrhythmia detection, was finetuned on 15 809 Massachusetts General Hospital patients.
issues.problem: The digest presents the model as using the ECG trace alone, when the published model also incorporated sleep stage data; it also omits that the network was pre-trained for arrhythmia detection and then fine-tuned on the MGH sample.
issues.suggested_fix: Add that the model combined the overnight ECG with sleep-stage information, and note the network was pre-trained for arrhythmia detection before being fine-tuned on the MGH cohort.

issues.label: "Free screen" overstates current applicability
issues.as_written: this suggests that data already being collected could double as a free cardiovascular risk screen without any extra test, visit, or cost
issues.abstract_says: Deep learning applied to nocturnal ECGs with sleep stage information captures cardiac abnormalities, offering a tool for cardiovascular risk stratification. Integrating such prediction into PSG could enhance detection and support personalized clinical decision-making.
issues.problem: The abstract describes a research tool that could potentially be integrated into polysomnography; calling it a free screen with no extra cost implies an available service and glosses over the processing, validation and implementation the authors frame as future work.
issues.suggested_fix: Rephrase as "could one day be used for cardiovascular risk stratification using data already collected, if the tool is validated and implemented in practice."

fact_check.headline: Dirty Air Appears to Speed Up Biological Aging — and Cleaner Air May Partly Reverse It
fact_check.notes: Description of the review, the biomarker hierarchy (Klemera-Doubal/PhenoAge/frailty most consistent, epigenetic clocks inconclusive), the mediation findings and the partial reversal with cleaner air all match the abstract; causal framing is appropriately hedged and the narrative-review limitation is flagged.
